source.title: Pharmacist: Safety Alignment Data Curation for Large Language Models Against Harmful Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Guo-Zhi Liu; Qi Mu; Tian-Sheng Huang; Xin-Hua Wang; Li Shen; Wei-Wei Lin; Li Zhang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether harmful fine-tuning affects safety using a harmful-output score, but the experiments and measure are not presented as a direct replication of the original study.
record.gate_note: The study fine-tunes safety-aligned models on user datasets containing varying proportions of harmful data, and measures unsafe outputs. The p=0 clean conditions use benign fine-tuning data, but there is no pre-user-fine-tuning reference score. It does not measure per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefilling, suffix attacks, decoding changes, or safety localization in weights or response depth. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper (Pharmacist data selection). Still, its Tables I/II report harmful score (HS) after user fine-tuning at harmful ratios 0 (clean), 0.05, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 of 1,000 examples. That gives a within-study dose-response bearing on V1. The setting is new: models are self-aligned with LoRA SFT on BeaverTails or RepNoise-Refusal, then fine-tuned on GSM8K mixed with BeaverTails harmful data.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: Pharmacist-selected alignment subsets improve resistance to harmful fine-tuning over Random and TaskVary, roughly match or slightly beat the full dataset, integrate with existing defenses, and cut alignment training time by over 50%.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a data-selection procedure for alignment and subsequent fine-tuning with varying harmful-data ratios; evaluates harmful-output rates and selection strategies rather than directly reproducing the original fine-tuning protocol and measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The harmful score changes with alignment dataset, data-selection strategy, model, and harmful-data ratio. The text also reports sensitivity to the number of harmful/validation samples and optimization settings.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
record.problems: No pre-user-fine-tuning harmful-score baseline is reported for the clean condition, limiting inference about benign fine-tuning erosion. No uncertainty estimates are stated. The paper's figures include additional plotted comparisons without tabulated values.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, omitted the remaining Table V results for Random and TaskVary selection, Table I repeated BeaverTails results, Table III task-specific results, fine-tuning accuracy and timing metrics, and figure-only time-course results in Figure 3. These are in Tables I, III, V and Figure 3; the omitted Table V selection-strategy values were excluded after keeping full-dataset and Pharmacist values for each defense.

untested.parts: Effect on professionally safety-trained chat models. The authors align base models themselves with LoRA SFT, and HS before user fine-tuning is not reported.
Whether benign fine-tuning raises HS relative to the aligned model before user fine-tuning.
Not tested; no per-token KL or position analysis.
Not tested; no prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
Not tested; no weight or rank localization.
Not tested; the study does not address why safety is shallow.
Not tested; no token-depth deepening training.

record.verdict_notes: Primarily a mitigation paper. The V1 evidence comes only from the harmful-ratio sweep in Tables I/II, using the clean p=0 condition as control. BeaverTails-aligned models are weakly safe even before harmful data (HS ~58%). Table I duplicates the BeaverTails half of Table II. The Figure 3 time-course of HS over fine-tuning steps is declared in rows_left_out. The alignment prompt description says outputs are 'real harmful response', likely a typo for refusal.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether refusal is removed almost entirely relative to a pre-fine-tuning baseline; tests harmful fine-tuning with 50–300 harmful examples in 1,000-example user datasets.

Reports harmful scores after benign-only fine-tuning, but does not compare them with the aligned model before user fine-tuning, so whether benign fine-tuning raises the score is not directly established.
Per-token KL and response-position concentration are not measured.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes are not tested.
No weight or rank localization experiment is reported.
The study examines data selection for robustness, not why safety would be shallow.
No training to spread safety across response positions or test of such deepening is reported.

relation.reason: Tables I–II report harmful-output rates after fine-tuning on 1,000 examples with zero or 50–300 harmful examples, rather than only comparisons between defense methods.

tranche.reason: Researcher-aligned models with different alignment datasets and selection methods provide a new setting; varying harmful ratios against matched clean fine-tuning directly measures V1.

source_check.notes: Clean columns describe models after benign user fine-tuning, not checkpoints before customization; these comparisons alone cannot establish V2. HS uses the BeaverTails moderation model on 1,000 held-out prompts; the checked tables provide no uncertainty estimates.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tested harmful-fine-tuning conditions, datasets, selection strategies, and models
reader_labels.reason: Unsafe outputs occur after fine-tuning with harmful examples, but the reported HS values are not evidence that refusal is removed almost entirely; results also vary markedly across alignment datasets and settings (R02–R05, R07–R10, R12–R15, R17–R20, R22–R25, R27–R30, R32–R35, R37–R40, R41–R58).
